extracted.intended_audience: British legislators, statesmen, and the educated public (late 18th-century readers of political commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and prescriptive standards for designing and judging government institutions (executive, judiciary, military, administrative) as argued in a political essay on the French Revolution. Emphasises independence, checks, and practical wisdom over theoretical novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive vigour and proper correspondence with supreme power
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive force must possess vigour and have a just correspondence or symmetry with the supreme power; an executive that lacks vigour or proper relation to the sovereign is a source of weakness and decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticises an executive that appears weak or unconformable to the supreme power, arguing such a mismatch prepares the state for ruin; the executive must be a proper instrument useful to its end rather than a mere pageant maintained at great expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful entrustment of the prerogative of peace and war
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of peace and war is the most dangerous prerogative and should not be left to the executive unless it enjoys other auxiliary trusts and checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive held additional auxiliary trusts to balance this power, advantages might compensate the risk; otherwise indirect correctives and controls (as in England) should be devised to prevent personal intrigues with foreign potentates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls to prevent foreign influence and intrigues
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be contrivances and controls upon the executive to keep foreign potentates from intriguing with members of the assembly and fomenting factions in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke suggests adopting indirect correctives similar to English institutions or inventing better ones; failing this risks foreign powers creating pernicious factions within the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers must possess confidence, authority, and discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers should have confidence from the sovereign (or proper appointing body) and real authority and discretion; mere subordinate servitude without power makes their office ineffective and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke describes ministers who are 'to execute, without power; ... responsible, without discretion; ... to deliberate, without choice' as inevitably betraying one or both sovereigns and themselves; ministers need real trusts and influence to serve the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent, permanent judicial bodies as safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial bodies (e.g., parliaments) that are independent and permanent provide certainty and stability to the laws, preserve the record of the constitution, and secure private property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke praises the old parliaments for being 'independent', holding office for life or by inheritance, constituting a corrective to arbitrary innovation and serving as a safe asylum for the laws across revolutions of humour and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elective, temporary, local judges for supreme judicial functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elective, temporary, local judges exercising dependent functions in narrow societies are the worst tribunals: they will be partial, fail to secure justice for strangers/minorities/the rich, and be susceptible to faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that such judges will not provide justice toward strangers or minorities and that ballot mechanisms intended to conceal inclinations instead produce suspicion and partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the power of remonstrance outside the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of remonstrance (to point out grievances and question decrees) should not be vested in the person who is to execute; remonstrance from the executor is absurd and confuses counsel and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues it was a mistake to vest remonstrance, formerly in the parliaments, in the principal executive officer (the king), because one should not allow remonstrance from he who is to execute—either the king must not have it or must have more power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from legislative orders and instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must not be sworn to obey rules, orders, and instructions from a legislative assembly that appointed them, because that converts judges into instruments of the governing power and removes legal ground for the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticises a system where judges are appointed to decide 'according to law' but are later told they will be given laws or must obey Assembly instructions; such judges become dangerous instruments capable of changing rules mid-cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should balance clarity with learned judicial discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: While laws should be 'short, simple, clear,' excessively short laws that discard legal learning will leave too much to judicial discretion and destroy the benefit of judicial learning in making sound decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that exploding the authority of the learning which produces 'sound discretion' defeats the purpose of law: removing judicial learning and experience undermines justice rather than improves it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies must be subject to law and accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative bodies (those executing public pecuniary trusts) ought to be strictly held to their duty and subject to the jurisdiction of tribunals, not exempt from the power of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke objects to administrative bodies being carefully exempted from jurisdiction; their exemption suggests they are being set up as sovereign independent states to enable leaders' progress from democracy to oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: High/state tribunals for offences against the nation must be independent
rubrics_metrics.description: A grand state judicature to judge crimes 'against the nation' must be formed in a spirit different from inquisition; if subservient to investigative committees it will extinguish liberty and settle arbitrary tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that unless great care is taken in composing such a tribunal—avoiding subservience to committees of research and removing its seat from the republic of Paris—it risks becoming an instrument of inquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army must remain an instrument, not a deliberative political body
rubrics_metrics.description: The army should be strictly an instrument subordinate to civil authority and not erect itself into a deliberative body acting by its own resolutions; otherwise the government may degenerate into a militant democracy which devours its creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke emphasises that when an army acts according to its own resolutions it becomes a political monster; discipline must be maintained so the military do not become a governing deliberative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clear chain of command and officer authority within the military
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers must retain authority and be respected; breakdowns where regiments violate laws, despise and drive away officers, or murder commandants indicate catastrophic loss of discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke gives examples (regiments refusing oaths, officers driven away, commandants murdered) to illustrate how a loss of officer authority renders the military unfit as an instrument of the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipalities and civic clubs must not supersede military authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal authorities and their societies should not arrogate authority over troops (trying officers, giving orders to soldiers, breaking them from posts), nor should troops be absorbed into civic clubs and feasts as a cure for indiscipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticises proposals to mix regiments with municipal clubs and civic entertainments—he argues such civic swearing and feasting may make soldiers 'admirable citizens' in the French mode but worse soldiers; municipalities superseding orders of the Assembly or king over troops is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proclamations and oaths alone are insufficient to restore military order
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating oaths, renewing decrees, and issuing proclamations are inadequate responses to military insubordination; substantive coercive measures (courts martial, inquiry into murders of commandants, breaking or decimating corps where necessary) are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke expects that severe measures will be necessary to arrest the worst evils; he criticises the Assembly for multiplying oaths and proclamations instead of taking decisive coercive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value experience and practical wisdom over abstract political regeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymaking should respect experience and the lessons of age rather than wholly embrace youthful, dogmatic schemes of political 'regeneration' or metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke derides the 'grand compounders in politics' who scorn old men and experience; he advises preserving the dignity and lessons of age and observation when constructing constitutions and institutions.
